claims.claim: Repeat length variation affects limb and skull morphology in dogs.
claims.source: Studies of individual or small groups of genes showed phenotypic consequences of repeat length variation on flocculation and cell adhesion in yeast (Voynov et al., 2006; Levdansky et al., 2007; Verstrepen et al., 2005), limb and skull morphology in dogs (Fondon and Garner, 2004) and on behavioral traits in voles (Hammock and Young, 2005).
claims.evidence: Experimental findings supported by citation.

claims.claim: Repeat length variation affects behavioral traits in voles.
claims.source: Studies of individual or small groups of genes showed phenotypic consequences of repeat length variation on flocculation and cell adhesion in yeast (Voynov et al., 2006; Levdansky et al., 2007; Verstrepen et al., 2005), limb and skull morphology in dogs (Fondon and Garner, 2004) and on behavioral traits in voles (Hammock and Young, 2005).
claims.evidence: Experimental findings supported by citation.

claims.claim: Recent advances in sequencing technology and STR-conscious alignment techniques now permit the detection and characterization of thousands of new STRs and their variation across the human genome.
claims.source: Recent advances in sequencing technology and STR-conscious alignment techniques now permit the detection and characterization of thousands of new STRs and their variation across the human genome, and have enabled genome-wide study of the effect of repeat length polymorphisms on gene expression (Willems et al., 2016; Payseur et al., 2011; McIver et al., 2011; O'Dushlaine and Shields, 2008; McIver et al., 2013; Willems et al., 2014; Mallick et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Technological advancement supported by citations to methodological studies.

claims.claim: STRs associated with differences in expression of nearby genes are called eSTRs.
claims.source: In homage to the expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) identified in traditional GWAS (Tam et al., 2019; Uffelmann et al., 2021), STRs associated with differences in expression of nearby genes are called eSTRs.
claims.evidence: Definition provided in the text with reference to analogous concept.

claims.claim: Repetitive elements can impact the transcription of neighboring genes or the genes in which they reside by regulating chromatin structure and epigenetic markers.
claims.source: Repetitive elements can impact the transcription of neighboring genes or the genes in which they reside by regulating chromatin structure and epigenetic markers.
claims.evidence: General mechanistic statement that will be supported by subsequent specific examples.

claims.claim: A role for repetitive DNA in facilitating 3D folding of the genome was first observed with TE-dependent formation of chromatin loops across multiple species, including yeast, Drosophila, and mammals.
claims.source: A role for repetitive DNA in facilitating 3D folding of the genome was first observed with TE-dependent formation of chromatin loops across multiple species, including yeast, Drosophila, and mammals (Figure 1(i); Cournac et al., 2016; Bourque, 2009; Lu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: Contact maps generated using chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) show high co-localization of repetitive elements in nuclear space in humans, mice, and Drosophila.
claims.source: Contact maps generated using chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) show high co-localization of repetitive elements in nuclear space in humans, mice, and Drosophila, demonstrating a structural function of repetitive DNA (Cournac et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Experimental observation from Hi-C studies supported by citation.

claims.claim: The enrichment of transcription factor binding sites in proximity to spatially associated repeats suggests that repeat-mediated 3D DNA packaging may allow for context-dependent co-transcription of linearly remote genes.
claims.source: The enrichment of transcription factor binding sites in proximity to spatially associated repeats suggests that repeat-mediated 3D DNA packaging may allow for context-dependent co-transcription of linearly remote genes (Cournac et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Inference from observed enrichment pattern supported by citation.

claims.claim: STRs play critical roles in maintaining chromatin structure.
claims.source: STRs play critical roles in maintaining chromatin structure (Nikumbh and Pfeifer, 2017; Sun et al., 2018; Volle and Delaney, 2012).
claims.evidence: General statement supported by citations to studies on STR-chromatin interactions.

claims.claim: Short CAG/CTG tracts avidly incorporate nucleosomes.
claims.source: For example, short CAG/CTG tracts avidly incorporate nucleosomes (Figure 1 (ii)), which are a basic subunit of chromatin packaging (Volle and Delaney, 2012).
claims.evidence: Experimental observation supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Nucleosome position varies with differences in STR length and flanking sequence context.
claims.source: Nucleosome position varies with differences in STR length and flanking sequence context (Volle and Delaney, 2012), influencing chromatin structure and transcription of nearby genes.
claims.evidence: Experimental finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: CGG repeats exclude nucleosomes in their native states, creating more open chromatin states near the transcription start sites of genes that favor local transcription.
claims.source: Other STRs, including CGG repeats, have the opposite effect and exclude nucleosomes in their native states, creating more open chromatin states near the transcription start sites of genes that favor local transcription (Wang et al., 1996; Wang, 2007).
claims.evidence: Experimental observation supported by citations.

claims.claim: The nucleosome exclusion feature of CGG repeats may underlie the enrichment of CGG repeats in promoters and 5'UTRs.
claims.source: This feature may underlie the enrichment of CGG repeats in promoters and 5'UTRs (Uesaka et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Inference from functional property supported by citation to genomic distribution study.

claims.claim: Some STRs are prone to methylation, which can lead to gene silencing and the absence of transcription.
claims.source: STRs can also influence chromatin structure by modulating DNA methylation. Some STRs are prone to methylation, which can lead to gene silencing and the absence of transcription (Quilez et al., 2016; Garg et al., 2021; Pappalardo and Barra, 2021).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic relationship supported by citations.

claims.claim: CpG islands are repeating di-nucleotide CpG sequences ranging from around 500–3000 base pairs and are located in ~40% of gene promoters across mammalian genomes.
claims.source: One common example of repeat-mediated gene silencing, CpG islands are repeating di-nucleotide CpG sequences ranging from around 500–3000 base pairs and are located in ~40% of gene promoters across mammalian genomes (Deaton and Bird, 2011; Janitz and Janitz, 2011; Thomson et al., 2010; Clouaire et al., 2012; Blackledge et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Genomic characterization supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: STRs are commonly located near CpG islands.
claims.source: STRs are commonly located near CpG islands (Sun et al., 2018), and may influence their methylation states (Figure 1 (iii)).
claims.evidence: Genomic distribution observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: STRs may influence CpG island methylation states.
claims.source: STRs are commonly located near CpG islands (Sun et al., 2018), and may influence their methylation states (Figure 1 (iii)).
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on proximity, illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Other STRs can contain CpGs within their repetitive sequence that can undergo methylation.
claims.source: Moreover, other STRs can contain CpGs within their repetitive sequence that can undergo methylation (Bolton et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Molecular observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: A genome-wide study in yeast estimates as many as 25% of promoters contain tandem repeats (TRs).
claims.source: A genome-wide study in yeast (Vinces et al., 2009) estimates as many as 25% of promoters contain tandem repeats (TRs).
claims.evidence: Quantitative finding from genomic analysis supported by citation.

claims.claim: Generally, expression of genes with TRs in their promoters increased with increasing repeat size.
claims.source: Generally, expression of genes with TRs in their promoters increased with increasing repeat size.
claims.evidence: General trend observed in the yeast study mentioned in context.

claims.claim: TRs in promoters may increase gene expression by increasing transcription factor binding, blocking or reducing nucleosome density, or in the case of AT-rich repeats, by facilitating DNA melting.
claims.source: TRs in promoters may increase gene expression by increasing transcription factor binding (Figure 1 (iv)), blocking or reducing nucleosome density, or in the case of AT-rich repeats, by facilitating DNA melting (Vinces et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic hypotheses supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Stable secondary structures formed by TRs can inhibit transcription by impeding procession and access of transcriptional machinery.
claims.source: However, stable secondary structures formed by TRs can also inhibit transcription by impeding procession and access of transcriptional machinery (Figure 1 (v); Grabczyk and Fishman, 1995; Belotserkovskii et al., 2010; Usdin and Woodford, 1995).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic observation supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The evolutionarily conserved THO complex is recruited to actively transcribed genes.
claims.source: For example, the evolutionarily conserved THO complex is recruited to actively transcribed genes (Kim et al., 2004; Abruzzi et al., 2004; Strässer et al., 2002), and facilitates elongation of RNA polymerase (Fan et al., 1996; Prado et al., 1997; Fan et al., 2001; Jimeno et al., 2002; Chávez et al., 2000) through super-helical structures formed by long GC-rich TRs (Voynov et al., 2006; Chávez et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Molecular mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The THO complex facilitates elongation of RNA polymerase through super-helical structures formed by long GC-rich TRs.
claims.source: For example, the evolutionarily conserved THO complex is recruited to actively transcribed genes (Kim et al., 2004; Abruzzi et al., 2004; Strässer et al., 2002), and facilitates elongation of RNA polymerase (Fan et al., 1996; Prado et al., 1997; Fan et al., 2001; Jimeno et al., 2002; Chávez et al., 2000) through super-helical structures formed by long GC-rich TRs (Voynov et al., 2006; Chávez et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Yeast strains with mutations to THO complex subunits exhibited lower levels of TR-containing FLO11 mRNA.
claims.source: Yeast strains with mutations to THO complex subunits exhibited lower levels of TR-containing FLO11 mRNA.
claims.evidence: Experimental observation from the yeast study described in context.

claims.claim: Reduced FLO11 mRNA coincided with an accumulation of RNA polymerase at the beginning of the gene.
claims.source: Reduced FLO11 mRNA coincided with an accumulation of RNA polymerase at the beginning of the gene.
claims.evidence: Experimental observation from the yeast study.

claims.claim: Removal of the TR or overexpression of topoisomerase I to enhance unwinding of the structured DNA, rescued the reduction in FLO11 mRNA in THO complex mutants.
claims.source: Removal of the TR or overexpression of topoisomerase I to enhance unwinding of the structured DNA, rescued the reduction in FLO11 mRNA in THO complex mutants (Voynov et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Experimental rescue result supported by citation.

claims.claim: Human STRs can either enhance and inhibit transcription of associated genes dependent on their sequence and locations.
claims.source: As in yeast, human STRs can either enhance and inhibit transcription of associated genes dependent on their sequence and locations, and also affect gene expression via changes in gene methylation and chromatin structure (Gymrek et al., 2016; Fotsing et al., 2019; Quilez et al., 2016; Garg et al., 2021; Jakubosky et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Summary of human STR effects supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Human STRs affect gene expression via changes in gene methylation and chromatin structure.
claims.source: As in yeast, human STRs can either enhance and inhibit transcription of associated genes dependent on their sequence and locations, and also affect gene expression via changes in gene methylation and chromatin structure (Gymrek et al., 2016; Fotsing et al., 2019; Quilez et al., 2016; Garg et al., 2021; Jakubosky et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic summary supported by citations.

claims.claim: STRs in RNAs form complex higher order structures, including G-quadruplexes and hairpins.
claims.source: STRs in RNAs form complex higher order structures, including G-quadruplexes and hairpins (Krzyzosiak et al., 2012; Sobczak et al., 2003; Malgowska et al., 2014; Sobczak et al., 2010), which are thought to exert broad influence over pre-mRNA splicing (Figure 1 (vi)) (Muro et al., 1999; Tu et al., 2000; Black, 2003; Solnick and Lee, 1987).
claims.evidence: Structural characterization supported by citations.

claims.claim: STR structures in RNA are thought to exert broad influence over pre-mRNA splicing.
claims.source: STRs in RNAs form complex higher order structures, including G-quadruplexes and hairpins (Krzyzosiak et al., 2012; Sobczak et al., 2003; Malgowska et al., 2014; Sobczak et al., 2010), which are thought to exert broad influence over pre-mRNA splicing (Figure 1 (vi)) (Muro et al., 1999; Tu et al., 2000; Black, 2003; Solnick and Lee, 1987).
claims.evidence: Inference from structural properties supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: An analysis of human introns found that sites of alternative splicing are enriched for STRs.
claims.source: An analysis of human introns found that sites of alternative splicing are enriched for STRs (Lian and Garner, 2005).
claims.evidence: Bioinformatic analysis supported by citation.

claims.claim: STRs can facilitate alternative splicing by complementary pairing of intronic repeats, bringing exonic regions into close proximity.
claims.source: STRs can facilitate alternative splicing by complementary pairing of intronic repeats, bringing exonic regions into close proximity (Lian and Garner, 2005).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic model supported by citation.

claims.claim: Structure-forming STRs can inhibit or enhance alternative splicing by blocking or facilitating the recruitment of splicing factors, respectively.
claims.source: Structure-forming STRs can inhibit or enhance alternative splicing by blocking or facilitating the recruitment of splicing factors, respectively (Lian and Garner, 2005).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic model supported by citation.

claims.claim: Alternative splicing of the EIIIB exon in the fibronectin gene is regulated by an intronic TGCATG repeat.
claims.source: For example, alternative splicing of the EIIIB exon in the well-conserved fibronectin gene is regulated by an intronic TGCATG repeat (Huh and Hynes, 1994; Lim and Sharp, 1998).
claims.evidence: Experimental finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Contractions in the TGCATG STR reduce EIIIB exon inclusion, while overexpression of a specific splicing factor, SRp40, stimulates inclusion.
claims.source: Contractions in this STR reduce EIIIB exon inclusion, while overexpression of a specific splicing factor, SRp40, stimulates inclusion.
claims.evidence: Experimental observation from the fibronectin study.

claims.claim: The TGCATG repeat can form a strong hairpin structure, which is a key feature of SRp40 binding site motifs.
claims.source: While the TGCATG repeat differs from SRp40's consensus binding site, it can form a strong hairpin structure, which is a key feature of SRp40 binding site motifs (Tacke et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Structural characterization supported by citation.

claims.claim: The TGCATG repeat may modulate alternative splicing by recruiting the SRp40 splicing factor to the intron/exon boundary.
claims.source: This suggests that the TGCATG repeat may modulate alternative splicing by recruiting the SRp40 splicing factor to the intron/exon boundary (Lim and Sharp, 1998).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic inference supported by citation.

claims.claim: Some STRs in RNA regulate splicing in trans, by binding to and sequestering splicing factors and blocking their functions.
claims.source: Some STRs in RNA regulate splicing in trans, by binding to and sequestering splicing factors and blocking their functions (Figure 1 (vii)).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic model illustrated in Figure 1, supported by subsequent example.

claims.claim: A recent study identified a group of novel long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) with multiple predicted RNA binding motifs, a subset of which contained long stretches of STRs ('strRNAs').
claims.source: A recent study identified a group of novel long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) with multiple predicted RNA binding motifs (Yap et al., 2018), a subset of which contained long stretches of STRs ('strRNAs').
claims.evidence: Discovery supported by citation.

claims.claim: The pyrimidine-rich noncoding transcript (PNCTR) contains numerous stretches of (TC)n repeats, avidly binds to the polypyrimidine tract-binding protein (PTBP1) in cells, and negatively regulates PTBP1-mediated splicing.
claims.source: One strRNA called the pyrimidine-rich noncoding transcript (PNCTR) contains numerous stretches of (TC)n repeats, avidly binds to the polypyrimidine tract-binding protein (PTBP1) in cells, and negatively regulates PTBP1-mediated splicing (Yap et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Molecular characterization and functional finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: PNCTR overexpression was sufficient to trigger mis-splicing of PTBP1 targets and trigger programmed cell death.
claims.source: As such, PNCTR overexpression was sufficient to trigger mis-splicing of PTBP1 targets and trigger programmed cell death (Yap et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Experimental result supported by citation.

claims.claim: STRs in RNA can regulate the global availability of other RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) with other functions, exerting profound control over numerous aspects of cell biology.
claims.source: In this way, STRs in RNA can regulate the global availability of other RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) with other functions, exerting profound control over numerous aspects of cell biology.
claims.evidence: General inference from the PNCTR example and broader context.

claims.claim: STRs in 3' UTRs can serve as RNA localization signals, and via interactions with RBPs, facilitate the transport of RNAs to specified cellular compartments.
claims.source: STRs in 3' UTRs can also serve as RNA localization signals, and via interactions with RBPs, facilitate the transport of RNAs to specified cellular compartments (Figure 1 (viii)).
claims.evidence: Functional role illustrated in Figure 1, supported by subsequent examples.

claims.claim: A program called REPFIND was developed to analyze 3' UTRs of localized mRNAs in Xenopus oocytes and identified various CAC-containing repeat motifs that serve as localization elements.
claims.source: A program called REPFIND was developed to analyze 3' UTRs of localized mRNAs in Xenopus oocytes and identified various CAC-containing repeat motifs that serve as localization elements (Betley et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Computational and experimental finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Mutating CAC-containing repeats was sufficient to abolish normal RNA localization.
claims.source: Mutating these CAC-containing repeats was sufficient to abolish normal RNA localization.
claims.evidence: Experimental result from the Xenopus study.

claims.claim: CAC-containing repeats were found in zebrafish and human 3' UTRs of transcripts that are known to be specifically localized within cells, suggesting that CAC-containing repeats are conserved localization elements in chordates.
claims.source: CAC-containing repeats were also found in zebrafish and human 3' UTRs of transcripts that are known to be specifically localized within cells, suggesting that CAC-containing repeats are conserved localization elements in chordates (Betley et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Comparative genomic finding and inference supported by citation.

claims.claim: REPFIND was used to generate a database of repeating motifs in 3' UTRs of mammalian genes from the Mammalian Gene Collection (MGC) that revealed hundreds of human genes containing short CAC- and CAG-rich repeats in their 3' UTRs.
claims.source: REPFIND was subsequently used to generate a database of repeating motifs in 3' UTRs of mammalian genes from the Mammalian Gene Collection (MGC) that revealed hundreds of human genes containing short CAC- and CAG-rich repeats in their 3' UTRs (Lim and Sharp, 1998).
claims.evidence: Bioinformatic analysis supported by citation.

claims.claim: CAC- and CAG-rich repeat elements facilitate RNA localization to neurites in rat hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Intriguingly, these elements facilitate RNA localization to neurites in rat hippocampal neurons (Andken et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Experimental finding in neurons supported by citation.

claims.claim: STRs located in 5' UTRs and coding regions impact mRNA translational efficiency.
claims.source: STRs located in 5' UTRs and coding regions impact mRNA translational efficiency.
claims.evidence: General statement to be supported by subsequent examples.

claims.claim: GC-rich STRs form stable RNA structures which can impede the processivity of scanning translational complexes.
claims.source: GC-rich STRs form stable RNA structures (Krzyzosiak et al., 2012; Sobczak et al., 2003; Malgowska et al., 2014; Sobczak et al., 2010), which can impede the processivity of scanning translational complexes (Figure 1 (ix)) (Kozak, 1980; Kozak, 1986; Kudla et al., 2009; Tuller et al., 2011; Ding et al., 2012; Bentele et al., 2013; Weinberg et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Structural and functional relationship supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: A native GGN repeat in the 5' UTR of the potassium 2-pore domain leak channel Task3 mRNA forms a G-quadruplex structure in vivo.
claims.source: For example, a native GGN repeat in the 5' UTR of the potassium 2-pore domain leak channel Task3 mRNA forms a G-quadruplex structure in vivo (Maltby et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Structural characterization supported by citation.

claims.claim: The G-quadruplex in Task3 5' UTR is inhibitory to translation of Task3 mRNA, but can be overcome by DHX36 helicase activity to improve ribosome processivity through the stable structure.
claims.source: This G-quadruplex is inhibitory to translation of Task3 mRNA, but can be overcome by DHX36 helicase activity to improve ribosome processivity through the stable structure (Maltby et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Functional characterization and mechanism supported by citation.

claims.claim: Libraries of synthetic and naturally occurring hairpin sequences placed within 5' UTRs can be used to precisely control translational transgene output.
claims.source: Indeed, libraries of synthetic (Millette et al., 2022) and naturally occurring (Li et al., 2017; Niederer et al., 2022) hairpin sequences placed within 5' UTRs can be used to precisely control translational transgene output, with potential implications for gene therapy dosing.
claims.evidence: Application supported by citations to synthetic biology studies.

claims.claim: Single unit variations in STRs can precisely modulate protein expression, generally permitting more and faster translation of mRNAs with smaller STRs, and less and slower translation of mRNAs with larger STRs.
claims.source: These studies show how single unit variations in STRs can precisely modulate protein expression, generally permitting more and faster translation of mRNAs with smaller STRs, and less and slower translation of mRNAs with larger STRs.
claims.evidence: Summary inference from the hairpin library studies.

claims.claim: Eukaryotic proteins are more likely to have repeats than prokaryotic proteins.
claims.source: Eukaryotic proteins are more likely to have repeats than prokaryotic proteins, and proteins containing repeats are often unique to eukaryotes and eukaryotic functions (Marcotte et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Comparative proteomics finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Proteins containing repeats are often unique to eukaryotes and eukaryotic functions.
claims.source: Eukaryotic proteins are more likely to have repeats than prokaryotic proteins, and proteins containing repeats are often unique to eukaryotes and eukaryotic functions (Marcotte et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Comparative analysis supported by citation.

claims.claim: Protein repeat domains typically serve as binding sites, and are thought to have evolved in eukaryotes to aide in the formation of multi-protein complexes with advanced cellular functions.
claims.source: Although their specific functions vary, protein repeat domains typically serve as binding sites, and are thought to have evolved in eukaryotes to aide in the formation of multi-protein complexes with advanced cellular functions (Andrade et al., 2001; Kajava, 2012; Sharma and Pandey, 2015).
claims.evidence: Functional and evolutionary inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: STRs translated into proteins are thought to serve as sites for protein-protein interactions.
claims.source: STRs translated into proteins, are thought to have similar functions as these larger repeat-based protein domains, serving as sites for protein-protein interactions (Figure 1 (x); Schaefer et al., 2012; Faux, 2012).
claims.evidence: Functional inference supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: CAG repeats are enriched in coding regions and are most frequently found in the polyglutamine (polyQ) reading frame.
claims.source: CAG repeats are enriched in coding regions and are most frequently found in the polyglutamine (polyQ) reading frame, suggesting that polyQ stretches in proteins have a native function (Schaefer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Genomic distribution analysis supported by citation.

claims.claim: The enrichment of CAG repeats in the polyQ reading frame suggests that polyQ stretches in proteins have a native function.
claims.source: CAG repeats are enriched in coding regions and are most frequently found in the polyglutamine (polyQ) reading frame, suggesting that polyQ stretches in proteins have a native function (Schaefer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Inference from genomic distribution pattern supported by citation.

claims.claim: PolyQ stretches are enriched in proteins that are components of multi-protein complexes, and have functions in transcriptional control, phosphatidylinositol (PI) signaling, protein degradation, and chromatin remodeling.
claims.source: PolyQ stretches are enriched in proteins that are components of multi-protein complexes, and have functions in transcriptional control, phosphatidylinositol (PI) signaling, protein degradation, and chromatin remodeling.
claims.evidence: Functional enrichment analysis from the cited study.

claims.claim: Evolutionary sequence comparison reveals that the location of polyQs within a protein is not always conserved.
claims.source: Evolutionary sequence comparison reveals that the location of polyQs within a protein is not always conserved (Schaefer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Comparative genomics finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: PolyQ stretches have evolved multiple times, and don't directly confer a protein's function, but rather modulate the protein-protein interactions necessary for those functions.
claims.source: This suggests that polyQ stretches have evolved multiple times, and don't directly confer a protein's function, but rather modulate the protein-protein interactions necessary for those functions (Schaefer et al., 2012; Orr, 2012).
claims.evidence: Evolutionary inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Other CG-containing STRs (i.e. CUGs and CGGs) show similar patterns of overrepresentation in coding regions and likely serve similar complex-scaffolding functions.
claims.source: Other CG-containing STRs (i.e. CUGs and CGGs) show similar patterns of overrepresentation in coding regions (Schaefer et al., 2012), and likely serve similar complex-scaffolding functions (Nasrallah et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Comparative analysis and inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Translation of a CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene (HTT) produces a polyQ tract in the HTT protein which serves as a flexible hinge, allowing the neighboring domains to fold into close proximity.
claims.source: For example, translation of a CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene (HTT) produces a polyQ tract in the HTT protein which serves as a flexible hinge, allowing the neighboring domains to fold into close proximity (Figure 1 (xi)) (Caron et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Structural characterization supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: HTT protein structure is altered with repeat expansion, demonstrating the importance of the flexibility conferred by the polyQ STR.
claims.source: HTT protein structure is altered with repeat expansion, demonstrating the importance of the flexibility conferred by this STR (Caron et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Structural analysis showing disease-related changes supported by citation.

claims.claim: Repeat expansions can alter local genome architecture and expression of neighboring genes.
claims.source: Repeat expansions can alter local genome architecture and expression of neighboring genes.
claims.evidence: General statement to be supported by specific example.

claims.claim: A CTG repeat expansion in the 3'UTR of the DMPK gene associated with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) alters local chromatin structure and suppresses transcription of neighboring gene, Six5.
claims.source: A prime example is observed at a CTG repeat in the 3'UTR of the DMPK gene associated with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), expansion of which alters local chromatin structure and suppresses transcription of neighboring gene, Six5 (Winchester et al., 1999; Brouwer et al., 2013; López Castel et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Experimental finding in disease context supported by citations.

claims.claim: CGG repeat expansions in FXS patients cause severe disruptions in chromatin boundaries.
claims.source: CGG repeat expansions in FXS patients cause severe disruptions in chromatin boundaries (Figure 2 (i); Sun et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Experimental finding supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Chromatin boundary disruptions may explain delayed DNA replication, activation of DNA replication stress pathways and altered local DNA replication patterns observed at CGG repeat expansions.
claims.source: These disruptions may explain delayed DNA replication (Subramanian et al., 1996), activation of DNA replication stress pathways (Chakraborty et al., 2020) and altered local DNA replication patterns (Gerhardt et al., 2014) observed at CGG repeat expansions and the Fragile X locus in particular.
claims.evidence: Mechanistic inference linking chromatin changes to replication defects, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Some STRs are aberrantly methylated only upon expansion.
claims.source: As genomic repeats influence native DNA methylation, some STRs are aberrantly methylated only upon expansion (Figure 2(ii); Otten and Tapscott, 1995; Steinbach et al., 1998; Herman et al., 2006; Greene et al., 2007; Belzil et al., 2013; Xi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Observation in disease contexts supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: When the CGG repeat in the 5' UTR of FMR1 expands beyond 200 repeats, it is susceptible to DNA methylation of both the CpG elements within the repeat and at a CpG element within the FMR1 promoter.
claims.source: When the CGG repeat in the 5' UTR of FMR1 expands beyond 200 repeats, it is susceptible to DNA methylation of both the CpG elements within the repeat and at a CpG element within the FMR1 promoter (Oberlé et al., 1991; Sutcliffe et al., 1992; Pieretti et al., 1991; McConkie-Rosell et al., 1993; Hansen et al., 1992; Coffee et al., 2002; Colak et al., 2014; Willemsen et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Molecular characterization in FXS supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Hypermethylation of the FMR1 CGG repeat is associated with FMR1 gene silencing, with a resulting absence of FMR1 mRNA and FMRP.
claims.source: This hypermethylation is associated with FMR1 gene silencing, with a resulting absence of FMR1 mRNA and FMRP, a critical RBP involved in synaptic plasticity and neuronal function (Oberlé et al., 1991; Hagerman et al., 2017; Quartier et al., 2017; Myrick et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Molecular consequence of methylation supported by citations.

claims.claim: The FMR1 locus remains transcriptionally active and unmethylated in human embryonic stem cells even in the presence of very large repeat expansions, with silencing occurring during differentiation.
claims.source: How exactly repeat expansion triggers methylation and the relationship between expansion, methylation, and epigenetic silencing is not fully understood, but the locus remains transcriptionally active and unmethylated in human embryonic stem cells even in the presence of very large repeat expansions, with silencing occurring during differentiation.
claims.evidence: Developmental observation indicating context-dependent silencing.

claims.claim: Some studies suggest that FMR1 silencing requires co-transcriptional binding of CGG repeat mRNA directly to the FMR1 promoter region as an RNA-DNA heteroduplex.
claims.source: Some studies suggest that FMR1 silencing requires co-transcriptional binding of CGG repeat mRNA directly to the FMR1 promoter region as an RNA-DNA heteroduplex (Colak et al., 2014; Groh et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations.

claims.claim: Premutation range CGG repeats which cause FXTAS or FXPOI result in elevated transcription of FMR1 mRNA.
claims.source: At FMR1, premutation range CGG repeats which cause FXTAS or FXPOI (and which are unmethylated) result in elevated transcription of FMR1 mRNA (Tassone et al., 2000a; Tassone et al., 2000b; Entezam et al., 2007; Brouwer et al., 2008; Kenneson et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Molecular observation in premutation carriers supported by citations.

claims.claim: Elevated FMR1 transcription in premutation carriers may result from use of additional upstream transcription start sites.
claims.source: This may result from use of additional upstream transcription start sites (Beilina et al., 2004; Tassone et al., 2011), or be associated with enrichment of acetylated histones or other chromatin activating factors at the premutation allele (Todd et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations.

claims.claim: Elevated FMR1 transcription may be associated with enrichment of acetylated histones or other chromatin activating factors at the premutation allele.
claims.source: This may result from use of additional upstream transcription start sites (Beilina et al., 2004; Tassone et al., 2011), or be associated with enrichment of acetylated histones or other chromatin activating factors at the premutation allele (Todd et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic hypothesis supported by citation.

claims.claim: It's possible that both hypo-expression and hyperexpression of FMR1 stems from the complex structures formed by CGG repeats as DNA.
claims.source: It's possible that both hypo-expression and hyperexpression of FMR1 stems from the complex structures formed by these CGG repeats as DNA (Usdin and Woodford, 1995; Fry and Loeb, 1994; Kettani et al., 1995; Patel et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Speculative mechanistic unification supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: Splicing of the HTT huntingtin gene is altered at expanded repeats associated with Huntington's Disease, resulting in the production of a transcript containing only exon 1 and the production of an exon 1 HTT protein.
claims.source: Splicing of the HTT huntingtin gene, which contains a CAG repeat, is altered at expanded repeats associated with Huntington's Disease, resulting in the production of a transcript containing only exon 1 and the production of an exon 1 HTT protein (Gipson et al., 2013; Sathasivam et al., 2013; Neueder et al., 2017; Neueder et al., 2018; Franich et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Molecular observation in HD supported by citations.

claims.claim: The exon 1 HTT protein is found in patient tissues and is toxic in model systems.
claims.source: The exon 1 HTT protein is found in patient tissues and is toxic in model systems (Gipson et al., 2013; Sathasivam et al., 2013; Neueder et al., 2017; Neueder et al., 2018; Franich et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Pathological observation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Incomplete splicing of HTT with the CAG repeat expansion increased with overexpression and decreased with knockdown of splicing factor SRSF6.
claims.source: Incomplete splicing of HTT with the CAG repeat expansion increased with overexpression and decreased with knockdown of splicing factor SRSF6.
claims.evidence: Experimental manipulation result from the HTT study.

claims.claim: SRSF6 is predicted to bind to the 5' end of HTT transcripts via the CAG repeat, suggesting that SRSF6-CAG repeat interactions interfere with spliceosome formation at the nearby splice site.
claims.source: SRSF6 is predicted to bind to the 5' end of HTT transcripts via the CAG repeat, suggesting that SRSF6-CAG repeat interactions interfere with spliceosome formation at the nearby splice site (Neueder et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic inference supported by citation.

claims.claim: Global splicing defects in REDs result from sequestration of critical splicing factors that bind to STR-containing RNA.
claims.source: Global splicing defects in REDs result from sequestration of critical splicing factors that bind to STR-containing RNA (López-Martínez et al., 2020; Mykowska et al., 2011; Botta et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic summary supported by citations.

claims.claim: RNAs with longer STRs bind more RBPs, which can cause a global cellular depletion of these factors.
claims.source: STRs can be binding sites for RBPs, regulating their availability throughout the cell. RNAs with longer STRs bind more RBPs, which can cause a global cellular depletion of these factors (Figure 2 (vii)) (Malik et al., 2021a; Glineburg et al., 2018; Rodriguez and Todd, 2019).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic principle supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: In myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), the expanded CTG repeat in the 3' UTR of the DMPK gene binds to muscleblind-like splicing regulator 1 protein (MBNL1) among other RBPs, resulting in depletion of critical splicing factors and global splicing defects.
claims.source: In myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), the expanded CTG repeat in the 3' UTR of the DMPK gene (López-Martínez et al., 2020; Korade-Mirnics et al., 1998; Udd and Krahe, 2012) binds to muscleblind-like splicing regulator 1 protein (MBNL1) among other RBPs (Paul et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2004; Fardaei et al., 2001; Mankodi et al., 2001; Miller et al., 2000), resulting in depletion of critical splicing factors (Botta et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2004; Pascual et al., 2006; Jog et al., 2012) and global splicing defects (López-Martínez et al., 2020; Paul et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2004; Du et al., 2010; Philips et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Well-characterized disease mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: RBP depletion by the CTG repeat in DM1 can also impact other aspects of pre-mRNA processing, including polyadenylation.
claims.source: RBP depletion by the CTG repeat in DM1 can also impact other aspects of pre-mRNA processing, including polyadenylation (Thomas et al., 2017; Goodwin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Extended mechanism supported by citations.

claims.claim: In FXTAS, premutation expansion mRNA sequesters and depletes multiple RBPs that bind to the CGG repeat RNA directly or indirectly.
claims.source: In FXTAS, premutation expansion mRNA sequesters and depletes multiple RBPs that bind to the CGG repeat RNA directly (i.e. DGCR8 Sellier et al., 2013), Purα (Jin et al., 2007), hnRNP A2/B1 (Jin et al., 2007; Iwahashi et al., 2006; Muslimov et al., 2011; Sofola et al., 2007) or indirectly via binding to CGG-bound proteins (i.e. Drosha Sellier et al., 2013 and Sam68 Sellier et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Multiple RBP interactions in FXTAS supported by citations.

claims.claim: CGG-sequestered RBPs are involved in a variety of functions including miRNA processing, mRNA transport, and splicing.
claims.source: These RBPs are involved in a variety of functions that are affected by their sequestration, including miRNA processing (DGCR8, Drosha), mRNA transport (hnRNP A2/B1, Purα) (Figure 2 (viii)), and in splicing (hnRNP A2/B1, Sam68).
claims.evidence: Functional roles of sequestered proteins, illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Splicing defects have been observed in CGG premutation expansion models.
claims.source: Splicing defects have been observed in CGG premutation expansion models (Sellier et al., 2010; He et al., 2014), but compensatory overexpression of CGG repeat-sequestered RBPs (Jin et al., 2007; Sofola et al., 2007; He et al., 2014; Qurashi et al., 2011) or blocking RBP binding to CGG repeats (Disney et al., 2012; Verma et al., 2019; Verma et al., 2020; Verma et al., 2022) can improve these disease-associated defects.
claims.evidence: Experimental observations and rescue experiments supported by citations.

claims.claim: Compensatory overexpression of CGG repeat-sequestered RBPs or blocking RBP binding to CGG repeats can improve disease-associated defects in CGG premutation models.
claims.source: Splicing defects have been observed in CGG premutation expansion models (Sellier et al., 2010; He et al., 2014), but compensatory overexpression of CGG repeat-sequestered RBPs (Jin et al., 2007; Sofola et al., 2007; He et al., 2014; Qurashi et al., 2011) or blocking RBP binding to CGG repeats (Disney et al., 2012; Verma et al., 2019; Verma et al., 2020; Verma et al., 2022) can improve these disease-associated defects.
claims.evidence: Therapeutic rescue experiments supported by citations.

claims.claim: Pathogenic sequestration of RBPs by expanded repeats mirrors the native role for STRs in RNA as RBP reserves, mediating fine-tuned dosing of RBP availability with repeat length.
claims.source: This pathogenic sequestration of RBPs by expanded repeats mirrors the native role for STRs in RNA as RBP reserves, mediating fine-tuned dosing of RBP availability with repeat length.
claims.evidence: Conceptual synthesis linking pathology to native function.

claims.claim: Expanded STRs in RNAs may cause toxicity by self-association (gelation).
claims.source: In addition to the depletion of RBPs and consequent defects in RNA splicing and localization and miRNA processing, expanded STRs in RNAs may also cause toxicity by self-association (gelation) (Figure 2(ix); Glineburg et al., 2018; Sellier et al., 2010; He et al., 2014; Jain and Vale, 2017; Ciesiolka et al., 2017; Fay et al., 2017; Tassone et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Pathogenic mechanism supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Phase separation properties of specific RNA motifs and their associated RBPs may exist on a spectrum from physiologic to pathologic.
claims.source: Yet, these processes also occur on RNAs with shorter STRs that are below the pathological threshold for disease, suggesting such that such phase separation properties of specific RNA motifs and their associated RBPs may exist on a spectrum from physiologic to pathologic.
claims.evidence: Inference from observation that gelation occurs at sub-pathological repeat lengths.

claims.claim: Expanded STRs in RNA can mis-localize or be retained in the nucleus instead of transported to its functional location in the cell.
claims.source: Expanded STRs in RNA can mis-localize or be retained in the nucleus instead of transported to its functional location in the cell (Davis et al., 1997; Mastroyiannopoulos et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Pathological observation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Nuclear retention of expanded STR RNAs may be mediated by splicing defects, via export-inhibiting RBP interactions, or via a larger dysfunction of nucleocytoplasmic transport.
claims.source: This may be mediated by splicing defects (Sun et al., 2015), via export-inhibiting RBP interactions (Smith et al., 2007), or via a larger dysfunction of nucleocytoplasmic transport (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Jovičić et al., 2015; Freibaum et al., 2015; Grima et al., 2017; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017; Sellier et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Multiple mechanistic possibilities supported by citations.

claims.claim: SRSF proteins bind to CGG and G4C2 repeats and appear critical to their cytoplasmic transport out of the nucleus.
claims.source: For example, SRSF proteins bind to CGG and G4C2 repeats and appear critical to their cytoplasmic transport out of the nucleus (Malik et al., 2021b; Hautbergue et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Molecular mechanism supported by citations.

claims.claim: Lowered expression of SRSF proteins or inhibition of the SRSF protein kinase SRPK1 suppress CGG repeat exit to the cytoplasm and reduce toxicity in Drosophila and neuronal model systems.
claims.source: In this context, lowered expression of SRSF proteins or inhibition of the SRSF protein kinase SRPK1, which regulates SRSF nuclear entry, suppress CGG repeat exit to the cytoplasm and reduce toxicity in Drosophila and neuronal model systems (Malik et al., 2021b).
claims.evidence: Experimental manipulation and rescue result supported by citation.

claims.claim: Scanning translational complexes are more likely to stall at stable secondary structures formed by expanded STRs.
claims.source: Scanning translational complexes are more likely to stall at stable secondary structures formed by expanded STRs (Figure 2 (x)), resulting in aberrant translation initiation upstream of or within the repeat in a process known as repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation (Figure 2 (xi)).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic model illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: RAN translation produces toxic peptides that contribute to expanded STR toxicity and neurodegeneration in numerous REDs.
claims.source: RAN translation produces toxic peptides that contribute to expanded STR toxicity and neurodegeneration in numerous REDs (Glineburg et al., 2018; Ciesiolka et al., 2017; Cleary and Ranum, 2017; Kearse and Todd, 2014; Kearse et al., 2016; Todd et al., 2013; Wojciechowska et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013a; Ash et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013b; Bañez-Coronel et al., 2015; Zu et al., 2011; Zu et al., 2017; Soragni et al., 2018; Ishiguro et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Pathogenic mechanism supported by extensive citations.

claims.claim: The mechanisms underlying RAN translation likely vary across different STRs and different genetic contexts.
claims.source: The mechanisms underlying RAN translation likely vary across different STRs and different genetic contexts (Malik et al., 2021a; Gao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Summary inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: At the CGG repeat of FMR1, RAN translation occurs in all three reading frames to produce polyarginine (FMRpolyR) (+0-frame relative to the AUG of FMR1), polyglycine (FMRpolyG) (+1-frame), and polyalanine (FMRpolyA) (+2-frame) peptides at different efficiencies.
claims.source: At the CGG repeat of FMR1, RAN translation occurs in all three reading frames to produce polyarginine (FMRpolyR) (+0-frame relative to the AUG of FMR1), polyglycine (FMRpolyG) (+1-frame), and polyalanine (FMRpolyA) (+2-frame) peptides at different efficiencies (Kearse et al., 2016; Todd et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Molecular characterization of RAN products supported by citations.

claims.claim: STR-induced stalling of translation machinery is responsible for a reduction in downstream production of FMRP in CGG premutation carriers.
claims.source: STR-induced stalling of translation machinery is also responsible for a reduction in downstream production of the main protein produced by FMR1 translation, FMRP, in CGG premutation carriers (Tassone et al., 2000b; Kenneson et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic explanation for reduced FMRP supported by citations.

claims.claim: Both FMRpolyG and FMRpolyA are present within intranuclear neuronal inclusions in patient tissues.
claims.source: At CGG repeats, both FMRpolyG and FMRpolyA are present within intranuclear neuronal inclusions in patient tissues (Sellier et al., 2017; Todd et al., 2013; Buijsen et al., 2014; Krans et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019), and are toxic in model systems (Sellier et al., 2017; Todd et al., 2013; Derbis et al., 2018; Gohel et al., 2019; Hoem et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Pathological observation in human tissue supported by citations.

claims.claim: FMRpolyG and FMRpolyA are toxic in model systems.
claims.source: At CGG repeats, both FMRpolyG and FMRpolyA are present within intranuclear neuronal inclusions in patient tissues (Sellier et al., 2017; Todd et al., 2013; Buijsen et al., 2014; Krans et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019), and are toxic in model systems (Sellier et al., 2017; Todd et al., 2013; Derbis et al., 2018; Gohel et al., 2019; Hoem et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Experimental toxicity findings supported by citations.

claims.claim: FMRpolyG is necessary for CGG repeat toxicity and inclusion formation in overexpression models.
claims.source: FMRpolyG, the most abundant CGG RAN product, is necessary for CGG repeat toxicity and inclusion formation (Sellier et al., 2017; Todd et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2015) in overexpression models.
claims.evidence: Experimental necessity demonstrated in models, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Numerous RAN or homopolymeric peptides generated in other REDs are essential for their toxicity and formation of proteinaceous inclusions.
claims.source: Numerous RAN or homopolymeric peptides generated in other REDs are essential for their toxicity and formation of proteinaceous inclusions (Figure 2 (xii); Yamamoto et al., 2000; Schilling et al., 1999; Ordway et al., 1997; Bäuerlein et al., 2017; Paulson et al., 1997; Mizielinska et al., 2014; May et al., 2014; Zu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: General principle across REDs supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Dysfunctional aggregation of repeat derived protein products mirrors the native function of STRs in proteins as facilitators of protein-protein interactions.
claims.source: Overall, dysfunctional aggregation of repeat derived protein products mirrors the native function of STRs in proteins as facilitators of protein-protein interactions.
claims.evidence: Conceptual synthesis linking pathology to native function.

claims.claim: Translation through large STRs that form stable secondary structures likely induces ribosome stalls and elongation errors.
claims.source: Translation through large STRs that form stable secondary structures likely induces ribosome stalls and elongation errors.
claims.evidence: Mechanistic inference from structural properties.

claims.claim: Disease-associated STRs undergo stall-induced translational frameshifting to produce novel chimeric polypeptides.
claims.source: A growing body of work shows that disease-associated STRs undergo stall-induced translational frameshifting to produce novel chimeric polypeptides (Gaspar et al., 2000; Toulouse et al., 2005; Davies and Rubinsztein, 2006; Tabet et al., 2018; McEachin et al., 2020; Wright et al., 2022), and several of these studies have shown that these frameshift products have distinct contributions to neuronal dysfunction in disease (Tabet et al., 2018; McEachin et al., 2020; Wright et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Emerging mechanism supported by citations.

claims.claim: Frameshift products from disease-associated STRs have distinct contributions to neuronal dysfunction in disease.
claims.source: A growing body of work shows that disease-associated STRs undergo stall-induced translational frameshifting to produce novel chimeric polypeptides (Gaspar et al., 2000; Toulouse et al., 2005; Davies and Rubinsztein, 2006; Tabet et al., 2018; McEachin et al., 2020; Wright et al., 2022), and several of these studies have shown that these frameshift products have distinct contributions to neuronal dysfunction in disease (Tabet et al., 2018; McEachin et al., 2020; Wright et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Functional characterization supported by citations.

claims.claim: Antisense transcription from the FMR1 locus generates multiple long-noncoding asFMR1 mRNAs, with some including the repeat.
claims.source: Antisense transcription from the FMR1 locus generates multiple long-noncoding asFMR1 mRNAs, with some including the repeat (Ladd et al., 2007; Khalil et al., 2008; Elizur et al., 2016; Pastori et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Molecular characterization supported by citations.

claims.claim: One antisense transcript, FMR4, is thought to play a critical role in regulating the cell cycle and apoptosis.
claims.source: One antisense transcript, FMR4, is thought to play a critical role in regulating the cell cycle and apoptosis (Khalil et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Functional characterization supported by citation.

claims.claim: Another antisense transcript, FMR6, is upregulated in premutation women, with increased repeat length correlating to elevated RNA levels and reduced number of oocytes.
claims.source: Another antisense transcript, FMR6, is upregulated in premutation women, with increased repeat length correlating to elevated RNA levels and reduced number of oocytes, suggesting a relationship between antisense transcript expression and toxicity (Elizur et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Correlation observed in clinical samples supported by citation.

claims.claim: The correlation between FMR6 expression and reduced oocyte number suggests a relationship between antisense transcript expression and toxicity.
claims.source: Another antisense transcript, FMR6, is upregulated in premutation women, with increased repeat length correlating to elevated RNA levels and reduced number of oocytes, suggesting a relationship between antisense transcript expression and toxicity (Elizur et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Inference from correlation supported by citation.

claims.claim: FMR1 antisense transcription is upregulated in Fragile X premutation disorders and lost in FXS, like the sense FMR1 mRNA.
claims.source: FMR1 antisense transcription in general is upregulated in Fragile X premutation disorders and lost in FXS, like the sense FMR1 mRNA (Ladd et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Expression pattern observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: AsFMR1 mRNAs containing the CCG repeats can undergo RAN translation, producing additional homopolymeric proteins with toxic potential.
claims.source: Moreover, asFMR1 mRNAs containing the CCG repeats can undergo RAN translation, producing additional homopolymeric proteins with toxic potential (Kearse et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Molecular mechanism supported by citation.

claims.claim: STR-containing antisense transcripts likely contribute to toxicity observed in many REDs, but this is best characterized in C9ALS/FTD and SCA8.
claims.source: STR-containing antisense transcripts likely contribute to toxicity observed in many REDs, but this is best characterized in C9ALS/FTD and SCA8, where antisense transcripts are found in toxic RNA foci and contribute to RAN peptide production (Mori et al., 2013a; Zu et al., 2011; Zu et al., 2013; Moseley et al., 2006; Gendron et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: General inference with specific examples supported by citations.

claims.claim: CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene are present in all humans at nonpathogenic lengths (<55 repeats) and conserved across mammals.
claims.source: While CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene were primarily studied for their disease association, the CGG repeat is present in all humans at nonpathogenic lengths (<55 repeats) and conserved across mammals (Eichler et al., 1995; Sellier et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Evolutionary conservation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Some studies suggest phenotypes associated with low CGG repeat numbers at the FMR1 allele in humans, including memory difficulties and language dysfluency.
claims.source: Some studies suggest phenotypes associated with low CGG repeat numbers at this allele in humans, including memory difficulties and language dysfluency (Klusek et al., 2018; Mailick et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Clinical associations at low repeat numbers supported by citations.

claims.claim: CGG RAN translation occurs in reporters with native repeat lengths (25 repeats).
claims.source: Our group observed that CGG RAN translation, originally thought to be an aberrant toxic event, occurs in reporters with native repeat lengths (25 repeats) (Kearse et al., 2016), suggesting CGG repeats and/or translation of those repeats may have a native function in addition to the pathogenic one.
claims.evidence: Experimental observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: CGG RAN translation at native and expanded STRs acts as an overlapping upstream open reading frame (uORF), inhibiting translation of the downstream main ORF and thereby reducing FMRP synthesis.
claims.source: CGG RAN translation at native and expanded STRs acts as an overlapping upstream open reading frame (uORF), inhibiting translation of the downstream main ORF (mORF) and thereby reducing FMRP synthesis (Rodriguez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic characterization supported by citation.

claims.claim: The RAN uORF-like regulation of FMRP synthesis was critical for facilitating translational changes associated with stimulation of metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) in neurons.
claims.source: Furthermore, this RAN uORF-like regulation of FMRP synthesis was critical for facilitating translational changes associated with stimulation of metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) in neurons (Rodriguez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Functional significance in neuronal signaling supported by citation.

claims.claim: Upstream open-reading frames (uORFs) are well-characterized regulatory elements in eukaryotes that influence expression of protein produced from the main open reading frame (mORF) on the same transcript, and are typically inhibitory to downstream mORF translation.
claims.source: Upstream open-reading frames (uORFs) are well-characterized regulatory elements in eukaryotes that influence expression of protein produced from the main open reading frame (mORF) on the same transcript, and are typically inhibitory to downstream mORF translation (Hinnebusch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Established molecular biology principle supported by citation.

claims.claim: uORFs resulting from RAN translation of STRs may play a global role in regulating mRNA translation.
claims.source: In this way, uORFs resulting from RAN translation of STRs may play a global role in regulating mRNA translation, presenting another mechanism by which STRs influence gene expression.
claims.evidence: Speculative generalization from the FMR1 example.

claims.claim: In spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), a CAG repeat expansion in the ataxin 1 (ATXN1) gene changes the localization of ATXN1 protein.
claims.source: In spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), a CAG repeat expansion in the ataxin 1 (ATXN1) gene changes the localization of ATXN1 protein (Irwin et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Disease-associated molecular change supported by citation.

claims.claim: ATXN1 normally shuttles between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, but an expanded polyQ region shifts ATXN1 localization to the nucleus.
claims.source: ATXN1 normally shuttles between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, but an expanded polyQ region shifts ATXN1 localization to the nucleus (Figure 2(xiii); Irwin et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Molecular characterization supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Aberrant nuclear localization of ATXN1 underlies dysfunction in SCA1.
claims.source: Aberrant nuclear localization of ATXN1 underlies dysfunction in SCA1 (Lam et al., 2006; Lai et al., 2011; Klement et al., 1998; Emamian et al., 2003; Duvick et al., 2010), as modifications that favor nuclear localization are sufficient to elicit disease relevant phenotypes in the absence of the repeat expansion in mouse models.
claims.evidence: Mechanistic causality supported by citations and genetic experiments.

claims.claim: Modifications that favor nuclear localization of ATXN1 are sufficient to elicit disease relevant phenotypes in the absence of the repeat expansion in mouse models.
claims.source: Aberrant nuclear localization of ATXN1 underlies dysfunction in SCA1 (Lam et al., 2006; Lai et al., 2011; Klement et al., 1998; Emamian et al., 2003; Duvick et al., 2010), as modifications that favor nuclear localization are sufficient to elicit disease relevant phenotypes in the absence of the repeat expansion in mouse models.
claims.evidence: Experimental sufficiency demonstrated in mouse models.

claims.claim: PolyQ-associated nuclear translocation is central to pathology in spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), where ligand binding and translocation to the nucleus of the expanded PolyQ-containing androgen receptor is required to elicit disease-associated transcriptional defects and cytotoxicity.
claims.source: PolyQ-associated nuclear translocation is also central to pathology in spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), where ligand binding and translocation to the nucleus of the expanded PolyQ-containing androgen receptor is required to elicit disease-associated transcriptional defects and cytotoxicity (Katsuno et al., 2006; Katsuno et al., 2002; Montie et al., 2009; Palazzolo et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Disease mechanism supported by citations.

claims.claim: Within the normal range of polyQ lengths observed in humans, Androgen receptor CAG repeat size inversely correlates with the receptor's transactivational activity and linearly correlates with infertility and decreased sperm function.
claims.source: However, within the normal range of polyQ lengths observed in humans, Androgen receptor CAG repeat size inversely correlates with the receptor's transactivational activity and linearly correlates with infertility and decreased sperm function (Choong and Wilson, 1998; Osadchuk et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Clinical correlations at normal repeat lengths supported by citations.

claims.claim: The correlation between androgen receptor CAG repeat size and function suggests that the CAG repeats play a normal role in testosterone activated gene cascades that become aberrant at larger repeat sizes.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the CAG repeats play a normal role in testosterone activated gene cascades that become aberrant at larger repeat sizes.
claims.evidence: Inference from the correlation data.

claims.claim: An investigation into dendritic mRNA localization identified a localization pathway dependent on the interaction of a CGG repeat-interacting RBP, hnRNP A2, with a GA dendritic targeting element of an RNA.
claims.source: An investigation into dendritic mRNA localization identified a localization pathway dependent on the interaction of a CGG repeat-interacting RBP, hnRNP A2, with a GA dendritic targeting element of an RNA (Muslimov et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Mechanistic discovery supported by citation.

claims.claim: The GA targeting motif was competed for by CGG repeat-containing RNAs, including FMR1 mRNA.
claims.source: This GA targeting motif was competed for by CGG repeat-containing RNAs, including FMR1 mRNA.
claims.evidence: Experimental observation from the dendritic localization study.

claims.claim: CGG repeats have a native function as a dendritic localization factor.
claims.source: In addition to a native function of CGG repeats as a dendritic localization factor, this study revealed that elevated levels of CGG repeat mRNA caused by the CGG premutation expansion sequester hnRNP A2, resulting in global dysfunction in the transport of hnRNP A2-target mRNAs (Muslimov et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Functional inference from the localization study supported by citation.

claims.claim: Elevated levels of CGG repeat mRNA caused by the CGG premutation expansion sequester hnRNP A2, resulting in global dysfunction in the transport of hnRNP A2-target mRNAs.
claims.source: In addition to a native function of CGG repeats as a dendritic localization factor, this study revealed that elevated levels of CGG repeat mRNA caused by the CGG premutation expansion sequester hnRNP A2, resulting in global dysfunction in the transport of hnRNP A2-target mRNAs (Muslimov et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Pathogenic mechanism linking native function to disease supported by citation.

claims.claim: A study seeking to reveal transcriptome-wide impacts of C(C)UG repeat-mediated MBNL depletion on splicing in myotonic dystrophy (DM) uncovered a global role for MBNL in mRNA localization.
claims.source: Another study seeking to reveal transcriptome-wide impacts of C(C)UG repeat-mediated MBNL depletion on splicing in myotonic dystrophy (DM) also uncovered a global role for MBNL in mRNA localization (Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Discovery from transcriptome-wide analysis supported by citation.

claims.claim: Autophagy induction results in clearance of polyQ aggregates, attenuating their toxicity.
claims.source: Numerous REDs are caused by CAG repeats, including the huntingtin gene in Huntington's disease (HD) and Ataxin 3 in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), with toxicity largely attributed to the aggregation of long polyQ containing proteins. Autophagy induction results in clearance of these aggregates, attenuating their toxicity (Rubinsztein, 2006; Ravikumar et al., 2004; Menzies et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Therapeutic mechanism supported by citations.

claims.claim: PolyQ tracts in ataxin 3 interact with beclin 1, a key initiator of autophagy.
claims.source: PolyQ tracts in ataxin 3, a deubiquitinase associated with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), interact with beclin 1, a key initiator of autophagy (Ashkenazi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Molecular interaction supported by citation.

claims.claim: Ataxin 3 deuniquitinates beclin 1, protecting it from degradation and permitting autophagy initiation.
claims.source: Ataxin 3 then deuniquitinates beclin 1, protecting it from degradation and permitting autophagy initiation.
